To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the scientific knowledge of Indian large felids is biased towards protected area settings and the biological sciences.

(i) the scientific knowledge on large felids in the Indian subcontinent is dominated by the biological sciences; (ii) the majority of this scientific knowledge is located in protected areas; (iii) there is a lack of knowledge on large felid conservation outside protected areas; and (iv) there is a need to understand the complex realities of large felid ecology in multi-use landscapes.
there is an ontological crisis in the scientific knowledge of Indian large felids.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the current body of research on large felids in the Indian subcontinent is adequate to inform conservation activity.
the ontological crisis in large felid research and management.

the ontological foundations of scientific knowledge and how these affect the production of knowledge about large felids in a multi-use landscape in India, and we argue that a more nuanced understanding of the ontological assumptions of science can help us to address these knowledge gaps.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current scientific knowledge base is inadequate to make informed decisions about the conservation of large felids, especially those that live outside protected areas.

the current scientific literature is not sufficient to inform conservation of large felids at the landscape level in India, and we need to move beyond a biological sciences–dominated approach that is based on a dualistic ontology of nature–culture.
the scientific knowledge base of large felids is not sufficient to inform conservation activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current body of knowledge on large felids in the Indian subcontinent has a limited utility for informing conservation policy and practice.
the present body of scientific knowledge is insufficient for the conservation of large felids.
the current scientific knowledge base of large felids is not sufficient for landscape level management decisions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we must recognise the importance of ontological diversity, and how this diversity can be used to generate new knowledge.

we cannot afford to ignore the ontological assumptions of science, which are often implicit and taken-for-granted, and that the knowledge base we use in making decisions about conservation needs to be more comprehensive, and include a range of knowledge forms, if we want our conservation efforts to be successful.
the scientific knowledge of the large felid community in India is currently insufficient to guide landscape-level management decisions.
